The Unseen Poem Is Always Paired

In some courses the unseen poem is a task on its own. In this course it is not. The unseen poem is printed beside a named poem from the anthology cluster you have studied, and the two are joined by a shared theme. Your job is to read the new poem quickly, then set it against a poem you already know well.

Your class studies one anthology cluster from a choice of three: Love and Relationships, Conflict, or Youth and Age. Each cluster holds fifteen poems written since 1789, mixing literary heritage poets such as Emily Brontë and Lord Byron with modern voices. Whichever cluster you study, the unseen poem you meet in the exam will be chosen to link to it thematically.

Key Fact

The poetry section is worth 40 marks and splits into two parts of 20 marks each. Part (a) compares a named anthology poem with a thematically linked unseen poem — both are printed for you. Part (b) asks you to explore one other poem from your cluster, chosen by you and written about from memory. Part (b) involves no comparison at all.

What the Question Actually Looks Like

Part (a) begins by naming both poems and telling you which is which. It then gives you a single comparative instruction — something like “Compare how these poems present the wish for an end to conflict” — followed by three bullet prompts:

  • ideas and attitudes in each poem
  • tone and atmosphere in each poem
  • the effects of the language and structure used

The bullets are there to shape your answer, and they tell you that method matters as much as meaning. Part (b) is worded more broadly: “Explore in detail one other poem from your anthology which presents…” and repeats the theme in a slightly broader form.

Love and Relationships ranges from John Keats’s sonnet ‘Bright Star’ and Emily Brontë’s ‘Love and Friendship’ to modern poems such as Rita Dove’s ‘Flirtation’ and James Fenton’s ‘In Paris with You’.

Conflict stretches from Mary Lamb’s ‘Envy’ and Lord Byron’s ‘The Destruction of Sennacherib’ to Denise Levertov, John Agard and Imtiaz Dharker. Note that the cluster is called Conflict, not War — a quarrel, an injustice or a divided mind all count.

Youth and Age includes William Blake’s ‘Holy Thursday’ and Theresa Lola’s ‘Equilibrium’. Whatever your cluster, learn its fifteen poems by theme as well as by title — part (b) is chosen by you, so pick the poem you can write about most confidently.

Which Skills Earn the Marks

Only two assessment objectives are credited in the poetry section. AO1 rewards a critical, informed personal response supported by textual references. AO2 rewards analysis of the language, form and structure a poet uses to create meanings and effects, with accurate terminology. In part (a), AO2 is the dominant objective. In part (b) the two carry equal weight.

Key Fact

Context is not assessed in the poetry section — you cannot know who wrote the unseen poem, so historical background earns nothing here. Neither is spelling, punctuation and grammar: that is credited in the Shakespeare section instead. Every mark in the poetry section comes from your reading of the poems and your analysis of how they work.

What Examiners Reward

Reports on this paper are consistent about what separates strong answers. The best responses engage confidently with the unseen poem, make comparison continuous rather than saving it for a final paragraph, and comment on the effect of a technique rather than simply naming it. They also answer the exact wording of the task without repeating that wording so often that it becomes intrusive.

The most common error is assuming that the two poets must agree. They frequently do not, and the differences between them are where the highest marks are earned. Read the unseen poem for how it departs from your anthology poem, not only for how it echoes it.

Writing about only one of the two poems in part (a). However good the analysis, a one-poem answer cannot rise past the lower bands.

Choosing a part (b) poem from a different cluster, or a poem that is no longer in the current anthology.

Re-using the part (a) anthology poem in part (b). It must be a different poem.

Comparing in part (b). Comparison is not required there, and it eats the time you need for close analysis of one poem.

How This Unit Works

The next three lessons build the analytical toolkit: language and imagery, then form and structure, then theme and personal response. Lesson five puts them together into the central skill of this paper: linking an unfamiliar poem to the cluster you know. The final lesson turns all of it into a timed routine.

Why Language Analysis Carries This Section

In the comparison part of the poetry section, analysis of the poet’s methods is the dominant objective. That means the marks come from explaining what a word does, not from naming a device. Examiners call the weaker habit feature-spotting. A response that lists metaphor, alliteration and enjambment without explaining any of their effects sits low in the bands, however many terms it uses.

Key Fact

Every analytical point should make three moves: quote a few words, say what those particular words suggest, then say why that matters to the idea the poet is building. Two images analysed this way earn more than ten techniques that are only named.

Imagery: What Is Being Transferred?

When you meet a simile or a metaphor, do not stop at naming it. Ask what qualities move from one thing to the other. Byron opens ‘The Destruction of Sennacherib’ with “The Assyrian came down like the wolf on the fold”. The simile gives the army a predator’s hunger and speed, but the more telling word is “fold”, which turns the victims into penned sheep: animals that are owned, counted and unable to escape. The slaughter is made to feel routine as well as violent.

An extended metaphor deserves even more attention. If a single comparison runs through a poem, it is almost certainly carrying the poem’s central idea, and it should anchor your response rather than appear as one point among many.

Personification gives human life to something that has none. In Wordsworth’s ‘Boat Stealing’, “a huge cliff” “Upreared its head” and, “with measured motion, like a living thing”, “Strode after” the boy. The cliff has not moved; the boy’s guilt makes it seem to. The personification turns the landscape into an image of the boy’s conscience.

Pathetic fallacy is the narrower case where weather or season mirrors feeling. Students spot it easily but often stop there. The mark comes from precision. Do not write “the rain shows sadness”; say what kind of sadness the particular weather implies.

Symbol is an object that carries meaning beyond itself. Watch for anything a poet returns to. A repeated object in a short poem is usually deliberate.

Connotation: Testing a Poet’s Word Choice

The most useful habit in unseen analysis is testing a word’s connotations against its alternatives. Emily Dickinson begins “There’s a certain Slant of light”. She could have written a beam, a shaft, a ray. “Slant” suggests something oblique and slightly wrong, and that crookedness prepares the reader for the pain the poem goes on to describe.

Ask yourself what would be lost if the poet had used the ordinary word instead. Your answer to that question is the point to write down.

Verbs repay this test more than any other word class. They carry the energy of a line, and poets choose them precisely. Whether a speaker walks, drifts, trudges or strides tells you almost everything about their state of mind, and the shift from an active verb to a passive construction often marks the moment a speaker loses control of their own story.

Semantic Fields

A semantic field is a cluster of words drawn from one area of life. Mary Lamb’s ‘Envy’ judges the envious mind with words of failed sight and sensation — the rose tree that cannot see “its own red rose” is called “blind and senseless”. Naming a semantic field is a strong move in an unseen poem because it lets you make one point about the whole text rather than a scattering of small ones.

Sibilance, the repetition of soft s sounds, can hush a line or make it hiss, depending on the context.

Plosives — b, d, p, t, k, g — stop the air abruptly and suit anger, force or shock.

Vowel length changes pace. Keats opens with “Bright star, would I were stedfast as thou art”, and the long open vowels hold the line steady, imitating the fixed star the speaker envies. Short vowels would have hurried it and destroyed the effect.

Key Fact

“The poet uses sibilance” earns nothing. “The soft s sounds slow the line to a whisper, so the threat seems to creep rather than strike” earns the mark. The difference is always the same: name the effect on the reader, and tie it to the poem’s idea.

Language Inside a Comparison

In the comparison part, resist analysing one poem’s language completely before turning to the other. Put the two images beside each other in the same paragraph. If one poet reaches for a predator and the other for a machine, that contrast is itself a point about attitude — and it earns credit under both objectives at once.

The Core Themes

A Christmas Carol braids together several interlocking themes. The most important are redemption, social responsibility, family, isolation, poverty, and the Christmas spirit. Thinking of these as a thematic web rather than a list means you can always move from one to another: Scrooge’s isolation is caused by greed, cured by memory, and transformed into family warmth. Good answers draw threads between themes, not walls around them.

Key Fact

The six key themes are: redemption, social responsibility, family, isolation, poverty and the spirit of Christmas. Colour-coding quotations by theme in your notebook is the fastest way to build a revision bank for the extract essay.

Redemption

Redemption is the novella’s structural backbone. Dickens shows it as a three-stage process: confrontation with the past (Stave 2), recognition of present harm (Stave 3), and fear of future consequence (Stave 4). The pattern echoes the Christian conversion narratives familiar to Victorian readers. Useful quotations: “I will honour Christmas in my heart”; “I am not the man I was.”

Social Responsibility and Poverty

Dickens wrote the novella in 1843, the year after the Second Report of the Children’s Employment Commission revealed the scale of child labour in Britain. The children Ignorance and Want are Dickens’s strongest argument that the middle and upper classes must engage with poverty. Link this theme to Scrooge’s “decrease the surplus population” (echoing Malthus), Marley’s “Mankind was my business”, and the Ghost of Christmas Present’s warning about Tim: “the child will die.”

Family appears through the Cratchits, Fred’s party and Belle’s later household. Each scene is a counterexample to Scrooge’s chosen isolation. Useful quotations: “God bless us, every one!” (Tiny Tim) and “my dear” (Mrs Cratchit, even in the face of Scrooge’s name).

Isolation is expressed through the adjective “solitary”, applied to Scrooge as a schoolboy and later as an adult. Dickens makes loneliness a self-imposed penalty: “as solitary as an oyster.” The Christmas spirit — “a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time” (Fred) — is the antidote.

Reading the Extract Question

On the novel question you choose one of two: an extract-based question that asks you to start with the extract and then explore the whole novella, or a discursive question with no extract. If you take the extract question, the command is clear: you must do both. A 5-minute plan should therefore map three sections — the extract, two supporting moments from other staves, and a final sentence linking everything back to Dickens’s argument.

Key Fact

Plan for 5 minutes, write for 40, check for 5. The plan should list: (1) extract thesis, (2) two methods from the extract, (3) two supporting moments from other staves, (4) context strand, (5) closing argument.

Structuring the 40-Mark Answer

Aim for four or five substantial paragraphs plus a sharp conclusion. A strong shape: Introduction (50 words stating Dickens’s argument); Extract paragraph (zoom in on two methods); Supporting paragraph 1 (a scene earlier in the novella); Supporting paragraph 2 (a scene later in the novella); Contextual paragraph; Conclusion (return to the statement given in the question). Treat the introduction as a miniature answer: state your line of argument, name the methods, and signpost context.

Use the authorial voice throughout: “Dickens shows...”, “Dickens suggests...”, “Dickens constructs...”. This automatically signals that you are analysing, not retelling.

Relevant context strands include: the 1834 New Poor Law and workhouses, Thomas Malthus’s ideas about population, Victorian ghost stories as moral warnings, Dickens’s own childhood in a blacking factory, and the Ragged Schools Dickens supported. Irrelevant context includes: biographical trivia about Dickens’s favourite foods, unconnected Victorian inventions, modern ideas of Christmas. The test is always: does this context change how I read the quotation?

Using Short, Embedded Quotations

OCR examiners repeatedly comment that the strongest candidates embed short quotations inside their own sentences rather than drop in long block quotes. Compare: ‘Dickens writes that Scrooge is “hard and sharp as flint”’ reads far weaker than ‘Dickens’s “flint”-like Scrooge is cold but capable of sparking change.’ Pick a single word or a three- to five-word phrase, slot it into your sentence, then analyse it. Aim for at least eight embedded quotations across a full essay — one or two per paragraph.

Final Checks Before You Submit

Run three final checks on your essay: (1) have you quoted from at least three different staves? (2) have you used the writer’s name at least once per paragraph? (3) does every quotation lead to analysis rather than paraphrase? Answer yes to all three and you are in the top bands. Manage time strictly — finishing a weaker answer beats abandoning a stronger one mid-paragraph. Common pitfalls to avoid: retelling the plot, writing about characters as if they were real, forgetting to use the author’s name, and leaving the conclusion empty or generic.

Exam Format Overview

The War of the Worlds question sits in the 19th-century novel section of your modern and literary heritage paper. It tests AO1 (response with textual references), AO2 (analysis of methods and effects), AO3 (context) and AO4 (accurate spelling and punctuation). This is typically a closed-text exam. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact format, mark weightings and timing.

You may face an extract-based question (analyse a given passage, then extend to the whole novel) or a discursive question (no extract; choose your own evidence). Both require clear argument, embedded quotations, and woven Assessment Objectives.

Key Fact

AO1 = response with textual references. AO2 = analysis of Wells’s methods and effects. AO3 = understanding of Victorian context (imperialism, evolution, class). Weave those three together rather than answering them in separate sections. AO4 also carries marks here for accurate spelling and punctuation.

Structuring an Analytical Response

Use the WHAT-HOW-WHY model: WHAT (state your point, AO1), HOW (analyse Wells’s method with a quotation, AO2), WHY (embed context, AO3). For Wells, key methods include: first-person narration, scientific register, imperial analogy, documentary realism, the anti-climactic ending.

Aim for 4–5 analytical paragraphs within the time allowed. Begin with a clear thesis and end with a brief conclusion linking back to your opening argument.

Imperialism: “Before we judge of them too harshly...” — narrator’s direct comparison. Technology: “a monstrous tripod, higher than many houses” — scale of threat. Human response: “that swift liquefaction of the social body” — civilisation’s collapse. Resolution: “slain by the humblest things” — ironic defeat.

Key Quotations to Memorise

Imperialism: “Before we judge of them too harshly we must remember what ruthless and utter destruction our own species has wrought.” Technology: “an almost noiseless and blinding flash of light” (Heat-Ray). Evolution: “slain by the humblest things that God, in his wisdom, has put upon this earth” (bacteria). Civilisation: “never before in the history of the world had such a mass of human beings moved and suffered together.”

Retelling the plot: the examiner knows the story. Every sentence should analyse, not narrate. Ignoring AO3: Wells wrote this novel specifically to critique imperialism — context is essential. Treating the novel as just an adventure story: always link events to Wells’s social purpose.

Key Fact

Memorise short quotations per theme: imperialism (“ruthless and utter destruction our own species has wrought”), technology (the Heat-Ray), evolution (bacteria), civilisation’s collapse (the London exodus). Practise embedding them in analytical sentences.

The Core Themes

Jane Eyre weaves a tight bundle of themes: independence, class, gender, religion, passion versus duty, and the Gothic or supernatural. Thinking of these as a thematic web rather than a checklist helps you to move confidently between them in an essay — Jane’s independence is bound up with her class position, which is shaped by Victorian gender expectations.

Key Fact

The six key themes are: independence, class, gender, religion, passion versus duty, and the Gothic. Build a quotation bank with one supporting line per theme — colour-coding helps in revision.

Independence

Independence is the novel’s spine. Brontë shows it as moral, financial and legal. Jane resists Mrs Reed (“I am not deceitful”), Rochester (“I am no bird”) and St John (“I scorn your idea of love”). Her inheritance turns the moral stance into a material one. Linking the theme to the Victorian coverture law shows why Jane’s financial autonomy is so hard-won — and so radical.

Class and Gender

Class and gender are intertwined. Jane is a poor, plain, unmarried woman working as a governess — a role Victorian society treated as awkward: educated but not a lady, paid but not respectable. Blanche Ingram represents the alternative: titled, beautiful, rich, but morally empty. Brontë pointedly allows Jane to win. When Jane asserts “I have as much soul as you, and full as much heart”, she refuses to let class and gender dictate her moral worth.

Brontë critiques Victorian religious fashions through three figures: Brocklehurst (hypocrisy), Helen (patient submission) and St John (rigorous duty). Jane rejects all three and instead creates a faith that allows love, equality and autonomy. Her marriage of practical Christianity is Brontë’s preferred model — religion lived through affection, not spectacle or repression.

Passion versus Duty

Brontë repeatedly tests Jane between passion (Rochester) and duty (St John). The novel argues that neither alone is sufficient. Jane’s refusal to become Rochester’s mistress is duty; her refusal to marry St John is passion; the final marriage is the balance of both. Use this dialectic to avoid reducing the novel to a love story: it is a moral argument about what love should be.

The Gothic and the Supernatural

The Gothic runs through every setting: the red room, the locked third storey, Bertha’s laughter, the split chestnut, the voice on the moor. Brontë uses these conventions not for decoration but to make a psychological point. Victorian women had few ways to express anger or desire directly, so the Gothic becomes the novel’s language of repressed emotion. Bertha is the most charged example.

Key Fact

Plan for 5 minutes, write for 40, check for 5. Your plan should list: (1) extract thesis, (2) two methods from the extract, (3) two supporting moments from other volumes, (4) one context strand, (5) conclusion linking back to the question.

Reading the Extract Question

The 40-mark question on the novel gives you a choice of two: an extract-based question that asks you to start with the printed passage and link to the whole novel, or a discursive question with no extract. Most candidates take the extract route, and a strong plan anchors you: a sharp opening that states Brontë’s argument; an extract paragraph; two supporting paragraphs from earlier and later in the novel; one contextual paragraph; a conclusion. Never leave the extract behind for too long — examiners want to see you moving between it and the wider text.

Using Context Properly

The best context is the shortest. A four-word phrase — ‘the 1840s coverture law’, ‘Evangelical moral rigour’, ‘colonial anxiety about Creole women’ — can unlock a quotation. What examiners hate is a standalone context paragraph that reads like a Wikipedia summary. Always tie context to a specific line.

Begin sentences with Brontë as the subject: ‘Brontë presents…’, ‘Brontë uses…’, ‘Brontë constructs…’. Saying ‘Jane decides’ describes the plot; saying ‘Brontë has Jane decide’ analyses the choice. This single grammatical shift is the quickest way to move from a middle to a high band.

Structural words are also useful signals of analysis: ‘juxtaposes’, ‘parallels’, ‘foreshadows’, ‘mirrors’. They announce to the examiner that you are thinking about how the novel is shaped, not just what happens.

Final Checks Before You Submit

Run three final checks. Have you quoted from at least three different parts of the novel? Have you used Brontë’s name at least once per paragraph? Does every quotation lead to close analysis rather than paraphrase? If yes to all three, you are in the top bands. Manage time strictly — finishing a weaker answer beats abandoning a stronger one mid-paragraph.

How the Comparison Task Works

This is the skill the poetry section is built around. You are given a named poem from your anthology cluster and an unfamiliar poem chosen to link to it, both printed on the paper, and a single instruction: compare how they present the theme the task names. All twenty marks depend on how well you keep the two poems together.

Key Fact

A response that writes about only one of the two poems — the anthology poem or the unseen one — cannot rise beyond the lower mark bands, no matter how skilled the analysis. Both poems must be present throughout. Analysis of method is the dominant objective in this part, so the comparison must be about how each poet writes, not only about what each poem says.

Step One: Read the Unseen Poem Through the Theme

Read the task first, then the unseen poem with that theme in mind. You are not trying to understand everything the poem does; you are trying to find what it says about the one idea you have been asked about. Annotate only against that idea. Time spent on anything else is time you will need later.

Step Two: Decide Whether They Agree

This is the decision that shapes the whole answer, and it is where responses most often go wrong. Students assume that because two poems are linked by theme, the poets must think alike. They frequently do not. A thematic link guarantees a common subject, not a common attitude.

Same idea, different feeling. Both poems may mourn a lost love, but one is bitter and one is calm. Use the shared idea to set up the paragraph, then make the difference in feeling your main point.

Same feeling, different method. Both poems build unease — one through broken lines and caesura, the other through a stanza that lengthens without reaching a full stop. When two poets reach the same effect by opposite means, that contrast makes excellent comparative writing.

Direct disagreement. Sometimes the unseen poem contradicts your anthology poem outright. Say so plainly, and build the whole response around that disagreement. This is the strongest structure available to you.

Step Three: Build a Grid in Five Minutes

Draw four rows down the margin of your answer booklet — idea and attitude, tone, language, structure — and two columns, one per poem. Fill it with short quotations only. Those four rows are the three bullet prompts the task gives you, split so that method has two rows instead of one. Each completed row is a paragraph, already comparative before you write a sentence.

Key Fact

Use the grid as your plan. Four rows — idea and attitude, tone, language, structure — and two columns, one for the anthology poem and one for the unseen poem. Five minutes spent filling it saves you from the block structure that costs marks, because every row already contains both poems.

Step Four: Write Alternately, Not in Blocks

The weakest structure discusses poem one for three paragraphs, then poem two for three paragraphs, then compares briefly at the end. The strongest is interwoven comparison: one comparative idea per paragraph, both poems inside it, evidence from each.

Comparative connectives carry that structure — whereas, by contrast, similarly, where one poet does this, the other does that. Use them honestly. A connective that promises similarity in front of a point that is really a contrast is worse than no connective at all.

A Worked Comparison

Suppose the anthology poem is Emily Brontë’s ‘Love and Friendship’ and the unseen poem is Thomas Hardy’s ‘Neutral Tones’, with the task asking how the poems present love that has failed.

Both poets judge love through the natural world, but they reach opposite verdicts. Brontë sets “Love is like the wild rose-briar” against “Friendship like the holly-tree”, then asks “which will bloom most constantly?” and uses the seasonal cycle to answer for the holly. Hardy allows no such consolation. His speaker recalls how “We stood by a pond that winter day”, and the pond offers neither renewal nor endurance — only stillness.

The comparison then moves to method. Brontë’s regular quatrains and simple similes make her argument feel settled, almost proverbial, as though the lesson has already been learned. Hardy’s image of a sun that is “white, as though chidden of God” drains the scene of warmth and colour, so that the failure of love is presented not as a lesson but as a stain the speaker cannot wash out.

Notice what the paragraph does not do. It never summarises either poem, it quotes no more than a handful of words at a time, and it never abandons one poem to deal with the other separately. Every sentence keeps both texts in view.

Three Things Not to Do

Do not summarise the poems before comparing them; the examiner has both texts in front of them. Do not save comparison for the conclusion. And do not invent context for the unseen poem — you cannot know who wrote it or when, and background earns no marks in this section anyway.

Theme 1: Belonging and Cultural Identity

Belonging is the play's central concern, and Pinnock argues that it requires accepting all parts of one's heritage — not choosing between Caribbean and English but holding both. Every character in Leave Taking struggles with where they belong. Enid belongs to neither Jamaica (which she left) nor England (which has never fully accepted her). Viv belongs in England linguistically and educationally but not emotionally. Del senses she belongs to a Caribbean heritage she has never directly experienced. Mai belongs fully to her Caribbean identity but is marginalised in English society.

Pinnock's resolution — fragile reconciliation rather than a neat happy ending — suggests that belonging is not a destination but a process. The family begins to hold both worlds without seeing them as contradictory. This is the play's most hopeful and most radical idea: hybrid identity is not a weakness but a strength.

Key Fact

The title 'Leave Taking' captures the theme of belonging. It refers to Enid's departure from Jamaica, the daughters' gradual departure from their mother's values, and — most importantly — the leave-taking from shame. Pinnock argues that immigrant families can only belong when they stop trying to leave their heritage behind.

Theme 2: Motherhood and Sacrifice

Motherhood runs through every strand of the play. Enid's motherhood is defined by sacrifice: she works exhausting hours, suppresses her own cultural identity and controls every aspect of her daughters' lives — all to give them a 'better' future. Her fierce protectiveness is driven by three things: her experience of an abusive marriage, her mother's death and their estrangement, and her experience of racism as a Windrush immigrant. Del's pregnancy introduces a new generation of the motherhood theme, and by the final scene Del has also become a kind of mother-figure-in-waiting — Mai's successor and Enid's bridge back to heritage.

The generational divide between Enid and her daughters mirrors the broader Windrush experience. The first generation sacrificed everything to build a life in England. The second generation questions the cost of that sacrifice. Pinnock shows both sides with sympathy: Enid's suppression comes from love, but it has created a void in her daughters' sense of self.

Crucially, Pinnock does not simply blame the older generation. She shows that Enid's choices were made in response to real racism and real economic hardship. The generational divide is not about one side being right — it is about understanding why each generation made the choices it did.

Racism is the backdrop against which every other theme plays out. Enid's assimilation is a response to racism. Mai's marginalisation reflects how Caribbean culture is dismissed by mainstream English society. Viv's sense of invisibility in the curriculum comes from a society that treats her heritage as inferior. Brod's disillusionment — and his account of how racism destroyed Del's father — shows the long-term human cost. Pinnock does not stage dramatic racist incidents: racism operates as a pervasive structural pressure shaping every character's choices.

OCR Exam Strategy

For OCR, Leave Taking is your modern prose or drama set text. The exam is closed text, so you cannot take the play in. You answer one question in two parts, and both parts are compulsory. Part (a) prints an extract from Leave Taking beside an unseen extract from another modern play, and asks you to compare them: 20 marks. Part (b) asks a related question on Leave Taking as a whole: 20 marks. Both parts reward AO1 (personal response), AO2 (methods) and AO3 (context). There are no marks for spelling and punctuation on this text. Plan carefully, and compare at the level of method, not just content — examiners reward analysis of how Pinnock makes meaning.

Key Fact

Key quotations and moments to prepare: Enid's insistence on 'proper' English; her grief after her mother's death in Scene 3; Brod's revelation about the abusive father in Scene 7; Del moving to Mai's bedsit; Viv walking out of her exam; Del reading Enid's palm in Scene 8; the candle symbolism; the two physical settings; the fragile reconciliation. Having 8–10 prepared areas allows you to adapt to any question.

Extract comparison strategy: Work through both extracts methodically — identify Pinnock's key language choices, dramatic techniques and structural decisions, then do the same for the unseen extract. Quote precisely from each. For every technique, explain its effect on the audience and connect it to the question's focus.

Whole-play strategy: Range across all eight scenes. Remember Leave Taking is a play: analyse dramatic techniques (naturalistic dialogue, code-switching, dual physical settings, Obeah scenes, silence, stagecraft) alongside language analysis. Integrate AO3 context (Windrush generation, 1980s London, racism) within your analysis, not as a separate paragraph.

Common mistakes to avoid: Plot retelling instead of analysing methods. Bolting context on separately. Forgetting it is a play. Referring to 'Act 1' and 'Act 2' when the play uses eight scene numbers. Only using examples from one part of the play. Identifying techniques without explaining their effect. Always focus on how and why Pinnock presents ideas, not just what happens.

What Character Analysis Means in Jane Eyre

Strong OCR answers on Jane Eyre treat characters as Brontë’s tools rather than real people. Each character is a vehicle for an idea about gender, class or faith. Your job is to analyse what she does with them: what quality they carry, how that quality changes, and what Brontë argues by showing us that change.

Key Fact

A character paragraph needs three moves: (1) the writer’s choice (‘Brontë presents…’), (2) a short embedded quotation, (3) a link to Victorian context or theme. Miss any one and the paragraph drops a band.

Jane: an Arc in Five Settings

Jane’s development is mapped onto the five main settings. At Gateshead she is the angry child (“I am not deceitful”); at Lowood she is the disciplined pupil learning from Helen and Miss Temple; at Thornfield she finds voice (“I am no bird”); at Moor House she is the independent heiress who refuses St John (“I scorn your idea of love”); at Ferndean she is the chosen equal (“Reader, I married him”). Treating the novel as a Bildungsroman lets you link geography to growth.

A useful revision task is to match one short quotation to each stage. Keep the quotations short — examiners reward embedded quotation over block quotes. Four words, accurately placed, beats a forty-word block quote.

Rochester begins as a Byronic hero — brooding, sardonic, secretive. Brontë uses him to interrogate Victorian ideas of male dominance. Track him in three phases: the mysterious master (Thornfield), the would-be bigamist (the interrupted wedding), and the humbled husband (Ferndean). He is never simply redeemed; rather he is rebalanced.

Useful quotations: “Bigamy is an ugly word”; “You have saved my life”; “it still renews hope”. Each corresponds to a different phase of his arc. Always attribute Rochester’s change to Brontë’s authorial purpose, not to his own decision.

Bertha: the Madwoman in the Attic

Bertha Mason is often treated as plot-furniture. She is actually Brontë’s most charged character. She is Jane’s doppelgänger: every time Jane represses rage, Bertha acts it out — the torn veil, the fires. She is also a figure of colonial violence: Brontë inherits and perpetuates Victorian language about Creole women that modern criticism (notably Jean Rhys and Gayatri Spivak) has interrogated.

A top-band candidate handles Bertha by holding two readings together: what Brontë intends (Bertha as Rochester’s past coming home) and what she accidentally reveals (the silencing of a Creole woman to secure a white heroine’s happiness). Both are legitimate; neither cancels the other.

St John Rivers: Cold Duty

St John is not villainous but wrong for Jane. Brontë uses him to show a second kind of temptation: a marriage of duty without desire. His “cold, cumbrous column” description is a physical metaphor for moral rigidity. Track his three roles: rescuer, cousin, suitor. Each role tests Jane’s autonomy.

Key Fact

Brontë builds a three-tier religious scheme: Brocklehurst (hypocritical), Helen (patient), St John (rigorous). None of them is a model for Jane, who creates a fourth model — faith with love — through her marriage.

Minor Characters as Moral Instruments

Helen Burns, Miss Temple, Mrs Reed, Grace Poole and Adèle all play small but weighted roles. The most useful technique is to ask: what does this character reveal when placed next to Jane? Helen’s patience exposes Jane’s fire; Mrs Reed’s cruelty sharpens Jane’s speech; Adèle’s vanity offers a child-version of Blanche’s adult shallowness. Brontë writes no minor character carelessly — each serves the novel’s argument.

Use a PEAL template. Open with Brontë’s intention; embed a quotation; zoom in on a single word; lift to Victorian context; link back to the question. The key difference from basic PEE or PEA is that L — the link — reminds the examiner you are still answering the original prompt.

Avoid biographical paragraphs (‘Brontë’s father was a clergyman’) unless the biography directly illuminates the line you quoted. Otherwise it becomes a detour that costs you time and earns no marks.

Building a Quotation Bank by Character

For every main character, aim to memorise four short quotations — one for each major stage. For Jane: ‘I am not deceitful’ (Gateshead), ‘soulless and heartless’ (Thornfield), ‘I am no bird’ (proposal), ‘Reader, I married him’ (ending). For Rochester: ‘Bigamy is an ugly word’ (wedding), ‘it still renews hope’ (Ferndean). For St John: ‘a cold, cumbrous column’ and ‘formed for labour, not for love’. Building these tiny banks per character means that in the exam you can pull an accurate phrase from memory without panicking about long recitations.

What a Personal Response Actually Means

The first assessment objective asks for a critical style, an informed personal response, and textual references used to support and illustrate interpretations. Notice the word informed. A personal response is not a feeling about the poem; it is an argument about what the poet is doing, held together by evidence. In part (b) of the poetry section this objective carries equal weight with analysis of method, so half of those twenty marks depend on having something to say.

Subject Is Not Theme

The subject is what happens in the poem. The theme is what the poet wants you to think about it. A poem whose subject is a soldier’s funeral may have grief as its theme, or waste, or the failure of ritual to comfort. Two poems can share a subject entirely and share no theme at all, which is why the comparison part rewards careful writing.

Key Fact

Before you write, compress your reading into a single thesis sentence: what is this poet saying, and how? Every paragraph then proves that sentence. Examiners consistently note that the strongest responses show clear signs of planning and establish an argument in the opening lines.

Read the Task Wording, Not the Poem Alone

Tasks in this section are precise. “Presents a satisfying relationship” is not the same as “presents a relationship”. “The wish for an end to conflict” is not the same as “conflict”. The qualifying words are the target, and they must shape which poem you choose in part (b) and which lines you quote.

Examiners also criticise responses that repeat the task wording so often it becomes intrusive, as well as those that ignore it entirely. Anchor the wording in your thesis and at the start of each paragraph, then let the analysis do the rest.

Take the task phrase and ask a question of it. If the task says “presents a difficult memory”, ask: difficult for whom, and why does the difficulty persist?

Answer in one sentence that names an attitude, not a topic. “The poet presents memory as a debt the speaker cannot repay, using the repeated imperative to make remembering feel like an order.”

Check that your sentence could be argued against. If nobody could disagree with your thesis, it is a summary rather than an interpretation.

Tone and Attitude

Tone is the poem’s voice; attitude is the position that voice takes. Keep the two apart. A poem can sound calm and still be furious. Watch for a tonal shift especially: a poem that begins tender and ends cold has given you a structural point and a thematic one in the same observation.

Pronouns are the quickest route into attitude in an unfamiliar poem. A speaker who moves from I to we is claiming to speak for a group; one who moves from you to they is stepping back from the subject. Tense does similar work: a poem told in the present tense makes an old wound feel current, while a sudden past tense can push a feeling safely out of reach. Both are observable in seconds and both point straight at what the speaker thinks.

Recognising Other Valid Readings

You are expected to recognise that different valid responses to a text are possible, and doing so is not hedging. Offering a second reading — “the silence could be grief, though it may equally be refusal” — shows critical thinking, and it is safer than asserting one meaning for a poem you met four minutes ago.

Key Fact

Part (b) is written from memory, and misquotation is expensive. Responses that lack textual support or misquote find the higher bands out of reach, particularly for analysis of method. Learn short quotations exactly — three or four words you can place perfectly are worth more than a whole line you half-remember.

For each poem in your cluster, learn one quotation for the central idea, one for the strongest image, and one from the ending. Three per poem is enough to write a confident part (b) answer.

Tag each quotation with a theme word rather than a poem title. When the task names a theme, you can then find your evidence by idea instead of hunting through titles under pressure.

Test yourself by writing the quotation out, not by reading it. Recognising a quotation is not the same as being able to recall it, and the exam asks for recall.

The Paper in Numbers

Everything in this lesson comes from three figures. The poetry and Shakespeare paper is two hours long, worth 80 marks, and taken closed text — no anthology, no play, nothing on the desk. Eighty marks in a hundred and twenty minutes gives you exactly one and a half minutes per mark, and every timing below is that figure applied.

Key Fact

The paper is two hours long and worth eighty marks. Forty marks go to the poetry section and forty to the Shakespeare section, so each deserves an even hour. Inside the poetry hour, part (a) and part (b) are worth twenty marks each — so they deserve thirty minutes each, planning included.

The Poetry Hour, Minute by Minute

0–5 min

Read the task, then both poems

Task first so you know the theme. Then read the anthology poem and the unseen poem, annotating only against that theme.

5–10 min

Fill the comparison grid

Idea and attitude, tone, language, structure — two columns, short quotations only.

10–30 min

Write part (a)

A comparative thesis, then three or four interwoven paragraphs. Both poems in every paragraph.

30–34 min

Choose and plan part (b)

Pick a different poem from your cluster and write your thesis sentence before you start.

34–58 min

Write part (b)

Detailed exploration of that single poem. No comparison.

58–60 min

Check and move on

Check quotations, then leave for the Shakespeare section on the hour whatever state the answer is in.

Key Fact

Part (b) is the most commonly rushed answer on this paper. Examiners report that responses are often brief, as if timing had been forgotten under pressure. It carries exactly the same twenty marks as the comparison. A thin part (b) costs as much as a thin part (a), and it is the easier of the two to fix.

Rubric Mistakes That Cost Whole Answers

A rubric infringement is a failure to read the instructions rather than a failure of skill, and it caps an answer that might otherwise have scored well. These four are the ones examiners see every year.

Answering on only one poem in part (a). The comparison must cover the anthology poem and the unseen poem together.

Choosing a part (b) poem from a different cluster, or one that has been removed from the current anthology. Check your cluster list before the exam, not during it.

Re-using the part (a) anthology poem in part (b). The task asks for one other poem, so the part (a) poem cannot be used again.

Comparing in part (b). No comparison is required there, and it steals the time you need for close analysis of one text.

What a Strong Answer Looks Like on the Page

Length does not earn marks. Examiners report very long scripts — some running to fifteen sides or more — whose quality suffered from their length, with the same point restated through one quotation after another. Three or four developed, interwoven paragraphs beat eight thin ones.

Keep quotations embedded and short. Four well-placed words prove more than a copied-out stanza, and they leave room for the analysis that actually earns the mark.

Two Practical Points About the Booklet

Spelling, punctuation and grammar are not assessed in the poetry section, so do not spend your final minutes proofreading. Legibility is a different matter: examiners regularly report scripts they struggle to decipher even when magnified. A mark cannot be given for a word that cannot be read.

Label your answers clearly as part (a) and part (b), and start part (b) on a fresh page. It costs nothing and it removes any doubt about which poem belongs to which task.

Week one. Untimed. Take an unfamiliar short poem, spend fifteen minutes filling a comparison grid against a cluster poem, and write nothing else. Grid practice is the highest-value drill there is.

Week two. Thirty minutes for part (a) alone, twice. Mark yourself on one question only: does every paragraph contain both poems?

Week three. Thirty minutes for part (b) alone, twice, on different cluster poems. Check your quotations against the text afterwards and count the misquotations.

Week four. The full poetry hour, both parts, in one sitting, twice. This is the only drill that tests whether you can stop part (a) on time.

The Final Check

Before you turn the page: does part (a) discuss both poems in every paragraph? Does part (b) cover a different poem from your own cluster, without comparison? Have you explained the effect of every method you named? If all three answers are yes, the answer is doing what the mark scheme asks.

What Character Analysis Actually Means

Character analysis in A Christmas Carol is not a biography. It is the skill of tracking how Dickens uses a character as a vehicle to carry a theme or argument. Examiners reward candidates who treat Dickens as an author making choices — not as a reporter describing real people. The central question is always: why has Dickens made this character behave, speak or develop this way?

Key Fact

Every strong character paragraph contains three moves: (1) the author’s choice, (2) a short embedded quotation, (3) a link to context or theme. Skip any one and the paragraph drops a level.

Scrooge: the Arc, Not the Person

Scrooge is Dickens’s central protagonist, and the most important thing about him is that he changes. A strong essay never describes him as “nasty” without also tracing his arc. Track him in five stages: Stave 1 (hard-hearted capitalist), Stave 2 (grieving the lost boy), Stave 3 (awakened to others), Stave 4 (confronted with death), Stave 5 (active giver). Every quotation you learn should be tagged to one of these stages.

Useful quotations across the arc: “Hard and sharp as flint” (the start), “I am not the man I was” (the turning point), “as merry as a schoolboy” (the rebirth). Notice that each quotation is short enough to embed in a sentence — examiners penalise long block quotes.

Bob is the novella’s working-class everyman. Dickens gives him patience (he tries to warm himself “at the candle” rather than complain), forgiveness (he toasts Scrooge) and grief (“He broke down all at once”). He is a foil to Scrooge: both are employees of the counting-house, but Bob embodies the warmth Scrooge rejects.

Tiny Tim is a symbolic figure of innocent vulnerability. His famous “God bless us, every one!” is recycled for the novella’s final line, linking him directly to the moral message. Dickens does not give Tim psychological depth because Tim’s role is not realism but moral weight: he is the test of Scrooge’s humanity.

Fred: the Positive Voice

Fred is sometimes overlooked in essays, but he opens and closes Scrooge’s transformation. His early definition of Christmas — “a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time” — is the thesis Dickens wants readers to accept, stated by a warm character before Scrooge can reject it. His persistent invitation, even after Scrooge’s refusal, models the forgiveness the novella argues for.

Key Fact

Characters in a Dickens novella are constructs used to argue ideas. Writing ‘Scrooge decided to change’ describes the plot; writing ‘Dickens has Scrooge change’ analyses the author’s choice — and that second phrasing is what separates top bands from middle ones.

Marley: the Warning Voice

Marley appears briefly but carries huge structural weight. His chain is the novella’s central emblem of greed, and his speech — “Mankind was my business” — states the novella’s moral argument before the plot develops it. Marley also functions as Scrooge’s double: what Scrooge will become if he does not change. Examiners reward candidates who notice this mirroring.

Belle appears only briefly, but her speech — “Another idol has displaced me; and if it can cheer and comfort you... I have no just cause to grieve. A golden one” — is the novella’s most explicit link between greed and spiritual loss. She chooses to leave with dignity, which strengthens her moral authority.

Fan, Mrs Cratchit, the laundress at Old Joe’s and the charwoman are Dickens’s briefly sketched women. Each occupies a narrow moral slot — loving sister, loyal wife, cynical thief — and serves a thematic rather than realist function. In an essay, treating Mrs Cratchit as Bob’s equal in protecting Tim’s memory is a strong AO1-style choice.

How to Organise a Character Paragraph

Top OCR answers use a PEA structure but go further. Open with Dickens’s intention (“Dickens presents Scrooge as a figure of modern capitalism in order to...”), embed a short quotation, zoom in on one word, then lift to context. Try this template: Dickens + presents + character + as + adjective + in order to + purpose. It forces analysis rather than retelling.

Avoid writing about characters as though their actions are choices made independent of Dickens. Instead of “Scrooge feels guilty”, write “Dickens shows Scrooge’s guilt through the repeated exclamation ‘Oh no, no!’”. This single re-phrasing is the quickest way to move from a middle to a higher band response.

Exam Format Overview

The Pride and Prejudice question is the 19th-century prose question, worth 40 marks. It assesses AO1, AO2, AO3 and AO4. The exam is closed text, so you will not have the novel in front of you. You choose one question from two: an extract-based question that links to the whole novel, or a discursive question. Spend about an hour on it.

Both question types require clear argument, embedded quotations, and woven Assessment Objectives. The examiner rewards responses that analyse Austen’s methods (irony, free indirect discourse, dialogue, symbolism) and embed Regency context within that analysis.

Key Fact

AO1 = ideas and textual references. AO2 = analysis of methods and effects. AO3 = understanding of context. AO4 = accurate, well-controlled writing. The examiner wants AO1, AO2 and AO3 woven together, not as separate sections.

Structuring an Analytical Response

Use the WHAT-HOW-WHY model: WHAT (state your point, AO1), HOW (analyse method with quotation, AO2), WHY (embed context, AO3). Begin with a clear thesis and aim for 4–5 analytical paragraphs, adjusting to the time you are given for the question.

Common mistakes: retelling the plot, bolting on context as a separate paragraph, writing about the novel without naming techniques. Every sentence should analyse Austen’s methods and their effects within a sustained argument.

Pride: “tolerable, but not handsome enough” — “My good opinion once lost is lost for ever.” Prejudice: “I could easily forgive his pride” — “Till this moment I never knew myself.” Marriage: “I ask only a comfortable home” — “You are too generous to trifle with me.” Class: “Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?”

Quotation Skills

Memorise short embedded quotations per theme: pride (“tolerable, but not handsome enough”), prejudice (“I could easily forgive his pride”), self-knowledge (“Till this moment I never knew myself”), marriage (“I ask only a comfortable home”), class (“Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?”).

Plot retelling: The examiner knows the story. Bolted-on context: embed it within analysis. Missing AO2: always name techniques (irony, free indirect discourse, dialogue) and explain their effect.

Key Fact

Short embedded quotations are more effective than long passages. Memorise 2–3 per theme and practise weaving them into analytical sentences.
